A.explanation: Laser light in an optic fibre is guided by total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary, not spreading round an obstacle.

B.explanation: Light forming images on a cinema screen involves projection and reflection from the screen, not spreading into a shadow region.

C.explanation: Waves spreading round the edge of the metal plate into the geometrical shadow is diffraction, which is strong when the obstacle size is similar to the microwave wavelength.

D.explanation: Sound simply travelling and spreading out as it moves through uniform air with no gap or edge is not diffraction.

hints: Notice which options include an obstacle or gap: only microwaves at the edge of a metal plate meets a sharp edge.
Recall diffraction is the spreading of a wave into the shadow region when it passes an edge, slit or obstacle of size similar to its wavelength.
Compare total internal reflection in the fibre and image projection on the screen with bending round an edge to see which matches the diffraction rule.
walkthrough: Identify the test: diffraction means a wave spreads out after passing a narrow gap or the edge of an obstacle, reaching places beyond straight-line travel.
Check option A: laser light travelling along an optic fibre stays trapped by repeated total internal reflection, so it is guiding, not diffraction.
Check option B: light waves forming images on a cinema screen are focused by a lens and then reflected diffusely by the screen, so no edge-spreading is described.
Check option D: sound waves diverging as they pass through air describes ordinary propagation in free space with no named slit or edge, so it does not show diffraction.
Check the remaining case: microwaves have wavelength of order centimetres, so passing the edge of a metal plate lets the wave bend round the edge into the shadow region.
That bending round an obstacle is exactly the cause-and-effect chain for diffraction. This is option C.
